d: Explains how using the MicroProfiler can help you optimize portions of your game.
h:
This walkthrough shows how to use the MicroProfiler to find a problematic aspect of a game and identify the root cause. Download the game, Open from File in Studio, and follow along.

Download the game


Identify the issue

  1. After you open the game in Studio, start testing it with F5 or the Play button.

  2. The frame rate feels decent, but not as smooth as it should be for a game of this size and scope. Press CtrlShiftF5 (⌘ShiftF5) to show the Performance Summary overlay.

Note that the frame rate is below 60 frames per second (FPS).

  1. Open the MicroProfiler by pressing CtrlAltF6 (⌘⌥F6).

Note that the frame times are consistent—the bars are roughly the same height—so whatever is causing the low frame rate is running every single frame as opposed to running occasionally and causing frame time spikes.

  1. Pause the MicroProfiler by pressing CtrlP (⌘P). Pausing with the keyboard shortcut opens detailed mode.

  2. Click and drag to pan the graph. Note how one particular task in the worker threads seems to be using a lot of processing time compared to the main thread. Hover over RunService.Stepped and note how long it's taking to render.

  1. Stacked bars in the timeline indicate a hierarchy of code, so keep hovering on lower and lower layers to try and identify the issue.

Note the LocalScript label, which indicates the name of the script, and the Raycast label, which indicates that the problem might be related to raycasting.

Create troubleshooting labels

Now that the MicroProfiler has provided a starting point, you can troubleshoot the problematic code.

  1. Stop the play test and filter the Explorer window for localscript to find the file.

A search for raycast indicates that this portion of code is probably the culprit for the game's poor performance:

```lua local RAYS_PER_SECOND = 1500

local function onStepped()

for _ = 1, RAYS_PER_SECOND do
    local startPosition = getRandomPosition()
    local endPosition = getRandomPosition()
    local direction = endPosition - startPosition

    Workspace:Raycast(
        startPosition,
        endPosition
     )
end

end

RunService.Stepped:Connect(onStepped) ```

Specifically, you can see that the code is casting 1,500 rays per second in random directions.

  1. To verify that this portion of code is causing the rendering delay, wrap the contents of the function with debug.profilebegin() and debug.profileend():

```lua local function onStepped()

  debug.profilebegin("Raycast Spam")

  for _ = 1, RAYS_PER_SECOND do
     local startPosition = getRandomPosition()
     local endPosition = getRandomPosition()
     local direction = endPosition - startPosition

     Workspace:Raycast(
        startPosition,
        endPosition
     )
  end

  debug.profileend()

end ```

Confirm and fix the issue

  1. Start testing the game, and open the MicroProfiler again.

  2. Note how the MicroProfiler now shows the custom label, indicating that this function was indeed the root cause.

  1. Stop the play test.

  2. Delete or comment out the onStepped() function and the RunService.Stepped:Connect(onStepped) connection.

  3. Start testing the game again, and check the Performance Summary again.

Note the huge improvement to frame rate and corresponding drop in frame times on the MicroProfiler graph.

kid.simple: This walkthrough shows how to use the MicroProfiler to hunt down a real slowdown. A sample game runs at about 45 FPS instead of 60. By pausing the profiler and hovering over the stacked bars, you find a LocalScript doing tons of raycasts every frame. You add a custom label to prove it, remove the bad code, and the game goes back to 60 FPS.
kid.analogy: It is like finding which app is draining your phone's battery. You check the battery screen, see one app at the top, close it, and the battery lasts longer again.
keyPoints: Download the sample game, open it in Studio with Open from File, and press F5 to playtest.
Press Ctrl+Shift+F5 to see the Performance Summary. The frame rate is below 60.
Open the MicroProfiler with Ctrl+Alt+F6. Bars of the same height mean the slowdown happens every frame, not just once in a while.
Press Ctrl+P to pause and open detailed mode. Drag to pan and hover over labels.
Stacked bars show what code is inside what. Hover deeper layers until you find labels like `LocalScript` and `Raycast`.
The culprit loops 1,500 raycasts every time `Stepped` fires.
Wrap suspicious code in `debug.profilebegin("Name")` and `debug.profileend()` to make your own label show up in the profiler.
Remove the bad code, test again, and confirm the frame rate is back to 60.

terms.MicroProfiler: A tool that shows how much time each task takes in every frame.
terms.frame time: How long one frame takes. At 60 FPS it should be about 16.67 ms or less.
terms.spike: A frame that takes much longer than the ones around it, shown as a tall bar.
terms.detailed mode: The MicroProfiler view that shows every task as a labeled bar on a timeline.
terms.worker thread: An extra helper line of work that runs alongside the main thread.
terms.raycast: Shooting an invisible line through the world to see what it hits. Each one costs some time, so 1,500 per frame adds up fast.
terms.Stepped: A `RunService` event that fires every frame before physics. Newer code uses `PreSimulation` instead.
terms.profilebegin / profileend: Functions in the `debug` library that mark the start and end of a chunk of code, so it shows up as its own named bar in the MicroProfiler.
terms.root cause: The real reason a problem happens, not just the symptom.

example.title: Label your own code in the MicroProfiler
example.code:
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local RAYS_PER_FRAME = 50

local function onPreSimulation()
	-- Everything between begin and end shows up as "My Raycasts"
	debug.profilebegin("My Raycasts")

	for _ = 1, RAYS_PER_FRAME do
		local origin = Vector3.new(math.random(-50, 50), 20, math.random(-50, 50))
		local direction = Vector3.new(0, -40, 0) -- straight down, 40 studs
		Workspace:Raycast(origin, direction)
	end

	debug.profileend()
end

RunService.PreSimulation:Connect(onPreSimulation)
explain: `debug.profilebegin("My Raycasts")` starts a named bar in the MicroProfiler.
The loop shoots 50 rays straight down from random spots 20 studs high.
`debug.profileend()` ends the named bar. Every `profilebegin` needs a matching `profileend`.
Open the MicroProfiler (Ctrl+Alt+F6) while playing and look for the My Raycasts label to see how long it takes. Raise `RAYS_PER_FRAME` and watch the bar grow.

watchOut: Forgetting `debug.profileend()`. Each begin must have an end, or the labels get mixed up.
Doing a lot of work inside a per-frame event. Even a small cost multiplied by 60 frames a second adds up.
Guessing instead of measuring. Use the profiler to find the slow part before changing code.
Leaving the fix untested. Always check the Performance Summary again after your change.
